title: SUPERSEDED - local egress bridge as the default transport
summary: SUPERSEDED by user instruction 2026-09-23, same day. Revision 1 concluded a browser cannot call these providers and made a local Node relay the default transport. The user rejected that outright: hit the real provider API directly, no /bridge/chat, no Python, and the real URL must appear in the network log. The technical evidence in this node remains CORRECT - Origin, Referer, User-Agent, Cookie and every Sec-* header are forbidden header names no JavaScript can set. What was wrong was the inference that this necessitates a relay. Those five headers are the ONLY thing a relay adds; the endpoint, body, wire format and credentials are all fully constructible client-side. Superseded by DECISION-20260923-direct-transport.

facts.claim: The error was not factual but inferential: from 'a browser cannot set five headers' I concluded 'therefore a browser cannot call this API'. Those are different claims. The headers a provider actually parses are the body and the endpoint, both settable. Whether a provider rejects cross-site is an empirical per-provider CORS question that should be TESTED, not pre-emptively routed around by inserting infrastructure the user did not ask for. Building the relay also cost the user a second process to run.

DECISION: static React SPA plus a local Node bridge on 127.0.0.1:8787. The SPA talks only to same-origin /bridge paths (proxied by Vite in dev). The bridge sets Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch-*, holds cookies and CSRF tokens, dials the provider, and relays the raw SSE back verbatim. Normalisation happens in the browser, so there is exactly ONE parser implementation.

BLOCKING EVIDENCE: all Sec- prefixed headers are forbidden request headers and cannot be modified from JavaScript (MDN Glossary 'Fetch metadata request header'; W3C Fetch Metadata spec section 4.2). Origin and Referer are likewise not script-settable. mCloudFlare, Dolphin and Mercury all send Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin; a browser will always send cross-site. All six providers send Origin and Referer.
evidence: bridge/headers.mjs lifted from DeepInfra.py 36-55, mCloudFlare.py 39-60, Dolphin.py 70-85, LLmChat.py 91-104, Inception.py 624-643

facts.claim: CORROBORATION: 'If you are calling one of these endpoints from frontend JavaScript - a client-side integration - your requests get rejected. The server sees Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site and Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors, and blocks you. From the browser, you can't change these headers. A server-side proxy can.' And: 'Server-side code (Node.js, Python, Go, etc.) also has no forbidden header restrictions.'

HONEST LIMIT: whether each provider actually ENFORCES those headers is UNKNOWN and could not be tested. All six provider hosts fail the TLS handshake in this sandbox (curl exit 35, SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL) while github.com and pypi.org respond normally, proving a targeted egress allowlist rather than general network failure. Some providers might ignore Sec-Fetch-* and accept cross-origin browser calls.
evidence: cors_probe2.sh: six providers curl_exit=35 http=000; two controls curl_exit=0 http=404/200

facts.claim: ESCAPE HATCH BUILT IN: every provider declares transport: 'bridge' | 'direct' in src/data/providers.ts. If the user confirms from a real browser that a provider returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin and ignores Sec-Fetch-*, that one provider can bypass the bridge with a single-field change. The UI, event model and normalisers are identical either way. The design does not require accepting the CORS conclusion; it allows testing it per provider.
REJECTED alternative 1 - pure static SPA calling providers directly: impossible for the reason above. Would have shipped something that cannot work.

REJECTED alternative 2 - a hosted proxy (HF Spaces, Vercel, Cloudflare Workers): reintroduces exactly what the user is trying to escape - one shared datacenter IP that gets blocked or rate-limited, plus hosting cost, uptime and sleeping. This is the 'powering issue' being removed.
evidence: user: 'not in the server formate in out of issue we do get the powering.. issuee'
the existing Dockerfile targets HF Spaces port 7860

facts.claim: REJECTED alternative 3 - a public CORS proxy service: routes user session cookies and CSRF tokens through an unaudited third party. Unacceptable for credential-bearing providers even before the deferred security review.
evidence: Upstage and Mercury both replay captured session material

facts.claim: REJECTED alternative 4 - normalise inside the bridge: would duplicate the parser in two languages (JS in the bridge, TS in the SPA) or force a build step on the bridge. Relaying raw SSE keeps the bridge dumb and the tested TS normalisers authoritative.
evidence: bridge/server.mjs pipes res.body verbatim into 'raw' envelope frames

facts.claim: TRADE-OFF ACCEPTED: the user must run a local process. Mitigated by zero dependencies (Node >=20 built-in http and fetch only), one command (npm run bridge), and an Offline Simulator provider so the UI is fully usable and demonstrable before the bridge or credentials exist.
evidence: bridge/server.mjs imports only node:http plus local modules

edges.target: agent, disclosed to user as a deliberate divergence from R4/R9
